tierWhy: instrument scoping measurement plus a source read of teardown loops; no money path, no product diff
surface: deployed http://31.97.192.82:3000, four-up, distinct datasets, PO workload armed
headline: THE INSTRUMENT IS NOT BLIND. Allocating 18 MB inside panel A's realm moved the HOST's usedJSHeapSize by 18.12 MB. Panels are same-origin, share one renderer process and one V8 isolate, and all four report the same heap. Every memory figure in the plan is scoped correctly for iframes.
oneLineAnswer: Yes, my harness reads the same API as the PO (performance.memory.usedJSHeapSize after a forced collection) — and it is NOT main-frame-only for our topology: a ballast allocated inside a panel iframe shows up in the host's reading, measured, one run, +18.12 MB for 300k objects.

instrument.name: MEMORY-API-SCOPE-V1
instrument.where: scripts/lib/heap-cycle-browser.mjs probeMemoryApiScope, behind --memory-api-probe (off by default; it allocates ballast)
instrument.contractTest: scripts/tests/heap-cycle-surface-dispatch.test.mjs now asserts memoryApiProbe reaches both surface dispatches — the option that a dropped dispatch voided a whole matrix with last time

measured.readingFromPerPanel: every panel reports a figure in the same 170-197MB band as the host, not its own small per-frame heap. A per-frame-isolated heap would read a few MB. They are all reporting the same shared isolate, sampled at different instants during a live replay.

ballastTest.reading: DECISIVE. The host's reading moved by the size of an allocation made entirely inside a panel realm.
ballastTest.honestCaveat: the post-release read (238.17MB) is higher than the post-allocation read because no collection was forced after the delete and the replay keeps allocating. That third number says nothing; only before-to-after does.

measured.corroboratingPriorEvidence: REALM-TAG-V1 and REALM-SURVIVAL-V1 already found panel-realm script sets (20.87MB) and the panel B realm inside snapshots taken from the HOST. A host-side snapshot cannot contain another isolate's objects, so panel realms were provably in the host isolate all along.

whatIsGenuinelyInvisible.workerHeaps: real blind spot — workers get their own isolate. Bounded, though: the census reads 1 live worker (created=1, terminated=0) and W-earlier closed '+1 once, not per cycle', so it is not the growing term. Closable cheaply via CDP Runtime.getHeapUsage against the worker target; named as next step.
whatIsGenuinelyInvisible.canvasAndGpu: real blind spot — not JS heap at all. GPU work was 23.87% of a core in the CPU census, so there is mass here, but it is not what usedJSHeapSize is for.
whatIsGenuinelyInvisible.crossOriginIframes: would be invisible under site isolation, but ours are same-origin, measured above.

measureUserAgentSpecificMemory.status: NOT AVAILABLE on the deployed surface

measured.reason: not a function on this surface

measureUserAgentSpecificMemory.why: the API is gated on cross-origin isolation, which needs COOP: same-origin and COEP: require-corp on the origin
warningBeforeAnyoneAddsThem: cross-origin isolation changes the process/isolate topology, so it changes the thing being measured mid-hunt

COEP require-corp blocks subresources without CORP headers, and the product depends on host-to-panel cross-frame access (frame.contentWindow.chart) that both the app and this harness use. Turning it on to measure memory could break the feature being measured.
it also resolves only after a collection and is coarse by design (bucketed, delayed) — it would give a per-frame breakdown I already have finer via per-realm snapshot attribution
measureUserAgentSpecificMemory.recommendation: do not re-instrument on it. The premise that motivated it — a blind gauge — is falsified above, and per-realm snapshot attribution is strictly finer than its per-frame breakdown. If the Director still wants it as a cross-check, it is a B headers ticket plus a re-baseline, not a swap.

consoleAttachedCost.askedFor: does the harness run with a console attached, and what does that cost
consoleAttachedCost.answer: Yes. The harness drives Chrome over CDP with the Runtime domain enabled, which is a console for retention purposes. I measured this in W81 and it is why deep console release is now the default before every floor sample.
consoleAttachedCost.mechanism: with the Runtime domain enabled the inspector holds page objects as '(Global handles) / DevTools console'. An Error created inside a panel realm closes over that realm via its stack accessor, so the session pins dead realms: 4 product-held against 8 console-held realms in the control.

magnitude.retroactiveCaveat: W84's own standard applies to this too: the MECHANISM is proven (console-held realms counted directly), the MAGNITUDE comes from one run per arm and is not settled. Do not quote -3.66 as the post-release rate; my n=3 pooled floor delta with deep release as default is 25-27 MB/cycle.
magnitude.shallowReleaseIsUseless: discardConsoleEntries + releaseObjectGroup both returned ok and freed nothing

consoleAttachedCost.consequenceForThePoFigures: the PO measured all night with DevTools open, and that inflates by this same mechanism. His ~12 MB/cycle is therefore an UPPER bound on the product's own rate, not an under-read. It does not explain the gap to my 25 — inflation pushes the wrong way for that — but it does mean nobody should treat his number as a floor.

forwardMutationCheck.askedFor: check the panel-teardown loop for forward mutation while iterating
forwardMutationCheck.result: NOT PRESENT in any teardown or purge loop in the sources I hold

loopsInspected.code: single get/delete by id, no iteration

loopsInspected.safe: keys snapshotted; React state Sets/Maps copied before delete

forwardMutationCheck.alsoAgainstTheSignature: the hypothesis predicts a deterministic skip: a forward splice over [A,B,C,D] removes A then C and skips B and D, so B and D would ALWAYS survive and C never would. I measure B always, A never, and C and D INTERMITTENTLY. It fits on A and B and contradicts on C.
forwardMutationCheck.limit: these are the local sources. I still do not hold the b99/b103 product tree, so I cannot rule the pattern out in the deployed build — the same gap as the escalated host-cache cut.

netEffectOnGrading: W84's retraction stands unchanged: A's five cuts measure as no effect at n=3, and the gauge that measured that has now been shown to see panel-realm allocations. The leak is not hiding from the instrument in the frames; the two places it could still hide are worker heaps (1 worker, not growing) and non-JS canvas/GPU memory.
